materials.title: The Wandering Mind: How the Brain Allows Us to Mentally Wander Off to Another Time and Place

credit.attribution: The Wandering Mind: How the Brain Allows Us to Mentally Wander Off to Another Time and Place — Julia W. Y. Kam. Frontiers for Young Minds. CC BY 4.0; complete original native paragraphs, whitespace normalised; media and third-party quotations excluded.
credit.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Article-specific original grant; images, quoted third-party text and excluded material omitted.

blocks.text: A unique human characteristic is our ability to mind wander—these are periods of time when our attention drifts away from the task-at-hand to focus on thoughts that are unrelated to the task. Mind wandering has some benefits, such as increased creativity, but it also has some negative consequences, such as mistakes in the task we are supposed to be performing. Interestingly, we spend up to half of our waking hours mind wandering. How does the brain help us accomplish that? Research suggests that when we mind wander, our responses to information from the external world around us are disrupted. In other words, our brain’s resources are shifted away from processing information from the external environment and redirected to our internal world, which allows us to mentally wander off to another time and place. Even though we pay less attention to the external world during mind wandering, our ability to detect unexpected events in our surrounding environment is preserved. This suggests that we are quite clever about what we ignore or pay attention to in the external environment, even when we mind wander.

materials.title: A Face Scavenger Hunt: Why We See Faces in Objects without Faces

credit.attribution: A Face Scavenger Hunt: Why We See Faces in Objects without Faces — Mary Nevins; Ashleigh Maxcey; Isabel Gauthier. Frontiers for Young Minds. CC BY 4.0; complete original native paragraphs, whitespace normalised; media and third-party quotations excluded.
credit.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Article-specific original grant; images, quoted third-party text and excluded material omitted.

blocks.text: Have you ever been playing outside and noticed a face popping out at you from the tree bark? Starting from birth, babies are immediately attracted to faces. Scientists were able to show this by having babies look at two simple images, one that looks more like a face than the other. By measuring where the babies looked, scientists found that the babies looked at the face-like image more than they looked at the non-face image [2]. Even though babies have poor eyesight, they prefer to look at faces. But why? One reason babies might like faces is because of something called evolution. Evolution involves changes to the structures of an organism (such as the brain) that occur over many generations. These changes help the organisms to survive. Some scientists, such as Carl Sagan, believe that face pareidolia helped humans survive because it made them alert to sneaky enemies [3]. By being able to recognize faces from afar or in the dark, humans were able to know someone was coming and protect themselves from danger.

In this account, reduced attention means the ability to detect unexpected events disappears. The preserved ability mentioned later must therefore refer only to thoughts inside the mind.

In this account, preserved detection of unexpected events means all outside responses and task performance remain unaffected. Research suggestions therefore establish that mind wandering has no negative consequences.

Earlier disruption and task mistakes remain possible. “Research suggests” marks how the explanation is presented; it is not proof of every response or an individual diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Which account keeps both the concession and the stated limits?
options: The account says poor eyesight prevents a preference for face-like images. The measured looking preference must therefore concern adults with good eyesight rather than the babies described.
The account treats the preference as proof that babies see perfectly and that evolution is the established cause. The words might and believe leave no uncertainty about that explanation.

The account reports a preference for face-like images despite poor eyesight. It offers evolution as a possible explanation, rather than showing that babies see perfectly or proving the proposed cause.

explanations.zh-Hans: 观察到的偏好属于婴儿，尽管文中说他们视力较弱；把观察移给成人颠倒了让步，也换了对象。

explanations.en: The observed preference belongs to the babies, even though their eyesight is described as poor. Moving the observation to adults reverses the concession and changes its participants.

explanations.zh-Hans: 偏好不证明视力完美；解释带有might及信念归属，不能把偏好或这种解释说成已证明的进化原因。
explanations.zh-Hant: 偏好不證明視力完美；解釋帶有might及信念歸屬，不能把偏好或這種解釋說成已證明的進化原因。
explanations.en: A preference does not establish perfect eyesight. The proposed explanation is explicitly qualified by might and belief, so neither it nor the preference proves an evolutionary cause.

explanations.zh-Hans: 视力较弱与观看偏好在让步中同时成立；测量比较的是婴儿看向哪里。might与some scientists…believe限定进化解释的强度。偏好、看得准不准、原因得到证明是不同主张。
explanations.zh-Hant: 視力較弱與觀看偏好在讓步中同時成立；測量比較的是嬰兒看向哪裡。might與some scientists…believe限定進化解釋的強度。偏好、看得準不準、原因得到證明是不同主張。
explanations.en: Poor eyesight and a looking preference coexist in the concession; the measured comparison concerns where babies looked. “Might” and “some scientists … believe” qualify the proposed evolutionary explanation. Preference, visual accuracy and proof of a cause are different claims.

blocks.text: In the morning early we continued our descent along a fine valley, with mountains rising 2,000 or 3,000 feet in every direction. The little river rapidly increased in size until we reached Senna, when it had become a fine pebbly stream navigable for small canoes. Here again the upheaved slatey rock appeared, with the same dip and direction as in the Sadong River. On inquiring for a boat to take me down the stream, I was told that the Senna Dyaks, although living on the river-banks, never made or used boats. They were mountaineers who had only come down into the valley about twenty years before, and had not yet got into new habits. They are of the same tribe as the people of Menyerry and Sodos. They make good paths and bridges, and cultivate much mountain land, and thus give a more pleasing and civilized aspect to the country than where the people move about only in boats, and confine their cultivation to the banks of the streams.

materials.title: Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None

blocks.text:
But it shall be your curse, ye immaculate ones, ye pure discerners, that ye shall never bring forth, even though ye lie broad and teeming on the horizon!

Verily, ye fill your mouth with noble words: and we are to believe that your heart overfloweth, ye cozeners?

But MY words are poor, contemptible, stammering words: gladly do I pick up what falleth from the table at your repasts.

Yet still can I say therewith the truth—to dissemblers! Yea, my fish-bones, shells, and prickly leaves shall—tickle the noses of dissemblers!

Bad air is always about you and your repasts: your lascivious thoughts, your lies, and secrets are indeed in the air!

Dare only to believe in yourselves—in yourselves and in your inward parts! He who doth not believe in himself always lieth.

A God’s mask have ye hung in front of you, ye “pure ones”: into a God’s mask hath your execrable coiling snake crawled.

Verily ye deceive, ye “contemplative ones!” Even Zarathustra was once the dupe of your godlike exterior; he did not divine the serpent’s coil with which it was stuffed.

A God’s soul, I once thought I saw playing in your games, ye pure discerners! No better arts did I once dream of than your arts!

Serpents’ filth and evil odour, the distance concealed from me: and that a lizard’s craft prowled thereabouts lasciviously.

But I came NIGH unto you: then came to me the day,—and now cometh it to you,—at an end is the moon’s love affair!

blocks.text: Triceratops species possessed a sturdy build, with robust limbs, and short five-hoofed hands and four-hoofed feet. Although certainly quadrupedal, the posture of these dinosaurs has long been the subject of some debate. Originally, it was believed that the front legs of the animal had to be sprawling at angles from the thorax, in order to better bear the weight of the head.

blocks.text:
“Is he married or single?”

“Oh, single, my dear, to be sure! A single man of large fortune; four or five thousand a year. What a fine thing for our girls!”

“How so? how can it affect them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” replied his wife, “how can you be so tiresome? You must know that I am thinking of his marrying one of them.”

“Is that his design in settling here?”

“Design? Nonsense, how can you talk so! But it is very likely that he _may_ fall in love with one of them, and therefore you must visit him as soon as he comes.”

“I see no occasion for that. You and the girls may go--or you may send them by themselves, which perhaps will be still better; for as you are as handsome as any of them, Mr. Bingley might like you the best of the party.”

“My dear, you flatter me. I certainly _have_ had my share of beauty, but I do not pretend to be anything extraordinary now. When a woman has five grown-up daughters, she ought to give over thinking of her own beauty.”

“In such cases, a woman has not often much beauty to think of.”

“But, my dear, you must indeed go and see Mr. Bingley when he comes into the neighbourhood.”

“It is more than I engage for, I assure you.”

“But consider your daughters. Only think what an establishment it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, merely on that account; for in general, you know, they visit no new comers. Indeed you must go, for it will be impossible for _us_ to visit him, if you do not.”

blocks.text:
“Christmas won’t be Christmas without any presents,” grumbled Jo, lying on the rug.

“It’s so dreadful to be poor!” sighed Meg, looking down at her old dress.

“I don’t think it’s fair for some girls to have plenty of pretty things, and other girls nothing at all,” added little Amy, with an injured sniff.

“We’ve got Father and Mother, and each other,” said Beth contentedly from her corner.

The four young faces on which the firelight shone brightened at the cheerful words, but darkened again as Jo said sadly, “We haven’t got Father, and shall not have him for a long time.” She didn’t say “perhaps never,” but each silently added it, thinking of Father far away, where the fighting was.

Nobody spoke for a minute; then Meg said in an altered tone, “You know the reason Mother proposed not having any presents this Christmas was because it is going to be a hard winter for everyone; and she thinks we ought not to spend money for pleasure, when our men are suffering so in the army. We can’t do much, but we can make our little sacrifices, and ought to do it gladly. But I am afraid I don’t,” and Meg shook her head, as she thought regretfully of all the pretty things she wanted.

“But I don’t think the little we should spend would do any good. We’ve each got a dollar, and the army wouldn’t be much helped by our giving that. I agree not to expect anything from Mother or you, but I do want to buy _Undine and Sintran_ for myself. I’ve wanted it so long,” said Jo, who was a bookworm.

generator.scope: Client generation preserving speaker, target, mixed attitude and epistemic limits on exact four inspected complete contexts; same-goal distinct-original application; complete raw source packages, no authored lessons or uninspected source approval.

teaching.en: Identify whose words or thoughts are presented and what they concern. Use the whole statement: praise, hopes, requests and regrets can coexist with hesitation or disappointment. Separate what someone thinks ought to happen from how they feel, and what they hope for from an achieved result. A character’s attitude does not automatically belong to another character, the narrator or the author. Keep the target, degree and qualifications instead of choosing a single emotional word out of context. Background: these are historical fictional family conversations, not instructions to adopt their social expectations. Establishment here concerns a household or settled position; engage for means undertake. A sacrifice gives up something wanted; gladly means willingly or cheerfully. Different family members may have different views.
teaching.zh-Hans: 先找是谁的发言或想法，以及它针对什么。结合完整陈述：赞许、希望、请求或遗憾，可以伴随犹豫或失落。区分认为应该发生什么与自己的感受，也区分希望与已成结果。人物的态度不会自动属于另一人物、叙述者或作者。保留对象、程度及限制，不脱离语境挑一个情绪词。 背景：这些是历史小说的家庭对话，不是要求接受其社会期待。establishment在此涉及家庭生活或安定处境，engage for是答应承担；sacrifice是放弃想要的东西，gladly是愿意或高兴地。不同家庭成员可能看法不同。
teaching.zh-Hant: 先找是誰的發言或想法，以及它針對什麼。結合完整陳述：讚許、希望、請求或遺憾，可以伴隨猶豫或失落。區分認為應該發生什麼與自己的感受，也區分希望與已成結果。人物的態度不會自動屬於另一人物、敘述者或作者。保留對象、程度及限制，不脫離語境挑一個情緒詞。 背景：這些是歷史小說的家庭對話，不是要求接受其社會期待。establishment在此涉及家庭生活或安定處境，engage for是答應承擔；sacrifice是放棄想要的東西，gladly是願意或高興地。不同家庭成員可能看法不同。

The caretaker supports the change while acknowledging a personal difficulty. This is neither complete opposition nor an announced successful trial; hope leaves the timing uncertain.

options: Mrs Bennet welcomes the possible marriage opportunity and presses her husband to visit. Her eagerness does not establish that Mr Bingley already intends to marry one of their daughters.
Mrs Bennet dislikes the possible marriage opportunity and urges her husband to avoid visiting. Calling the prospect a fine thing expresses her rejection of the proposed visit.
Mrs Bennet calmly reports an agreed marriage plan from Mr Bingley. Her words very likely and may confirm that he has already decided which daughter he will marry.

explanations.zh-Hans: 这把欢迎与坚持颠倒了：她说机会很好，反复要求拜访，并非反对。

explanations.en: This reverses her expressed welcome and insistence: she calls the opportunity fine and repeatedly asks for the visit, rather than rejecting it.

explanations.en: Expectation is not an agreed plan. She explicitly treats his falling in love as a possibility, and names no daughter already chosen by him.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation keeps the speaker’s attitude and its limits?
options: Meg welcomes giving everything up without disappointment. Saying they ought to do it gladly establishes that she already feels entirely cheerful about the sacrifice.
Meg rejects the reason for any sacrifice and says their mother’s concern has no value. Her disappointment proves she denies that they ought to give up any pleasure.
Meg accepts the reason for small sacrifices but admits she does not feel glad about giving things up. Her attitude mixes a sense of what they ought to do with personal disappointment.

explanations.zh-Hans: ought说的是她认为应该怎样，并非已经有什么感受；后面的承认与遗憾排除了毫无失落的高兴。
explanations.zh-Hant: ought說的是她認為應該怎樣，並非已經有什麼感受；後面的承認與遺憾排除了毫無失落的高興。
explanations.en: Ought expresses what she thinks they should do, not how she already feels. The following admission and regret explicitly rule out uncomplicated cheerfulness.

explanations.zh-Hans: 个人失落不取消她承认的理由与责任；这个选项把复杂态度改成全盘否定，还移用了另一人的异议。
explanations.zh-Hant: 個人失落不取消她承認的理由與責任；這個選項把複雜態度改成全盤否定，還移用了另一人的異議。
explanations.en: Personal disappointment does not erase her stated reason or duty. The option changes a mixed attitude into complete rejection and borrows an objection from another speaker.

explanations.zh-Hans: Meg解释严冬与军人的艰难，说应作小小牺牲，随后承认I am afraid I don’t，接的是并不觉得高兴。舍不得想要的东西，与承认责任可以并存。后面Jo的异议属于另一个人物，不能移给Meg。
explanations.zh-Hant: Meg解釋嚴冬與軍人的艱難，說應作小小犧牲，隨後承認I am afraid I don’t，接的是並不覺得高興。捨不得想要的東西，與承認責任可以並存。後面Jo的異議屬於另一個人物，不能移給Meg。
explanations.en: Meg explains the hard winter and soldiers’ hardship, says they ought to make small sacrifices, then admits “I am afraid I don’t” feel glad. Her regret about wanted things coexists with that stated duty. Jo’s later objection is another character’s view; do not transfer it to Meg.

blocks.text: I have discovered a new dramatist, and I am going to produce a play of his within three months, I hope. I shan't tell you his name and I shan't tell you anything about the play, except that I find more promise in it than anything I have seen or read for months.

teaching.en: Identify whose words or thoughts are presented and what they concern. Use the whole statement: praise, hopes, requests and regrets can coexist with hesitation or disappointment. Separate what someone thinks ought to happen from how they feel, and what they hope for from an achieved result. A character’s attitude does not automatically belong to another character, the narrator or the author. Keep the target, degree and qualifications instead of choosing a single emotional word out of context. Background: a dramatist writes plays; produce a play means arrange its staging. Promise can mean potential. A composition is a created piece, such as a song; a manuscript is a written copy; crude here means unpolished. A fictional speech and a memoir narrator’s reflection are different voices; neither is automatically the recording reader’s opinion.
teaching.zh-Hans: 先找是谁的发言或想法，以及它针对什么。结合完整陈述：赞许、希望、请求或遗憾，可以伴随犹豫或失落。区分认为应该发生什么与自己的感受，也区分希望与已成结果。人物的态度不会自动属于另一人物、叙述者或作者。保留对象、程度及限制，不脱离语境挑一个情绪词。 背景：dramatist是剧作家，produce a play是筹办演出，promise可以指潜力。composition是创作的作品，如歌曲，manuscript是文字稿，crude在此指粗糙。小说人物发言与回忆录叙述者的反思是不同声音，都不自动等于录音朗读者的意见。
teaching.zh-Hant: 先找是誰的發言或想法，以及它針對什麼。結合完整陳述：讚許、希望、請求或遺憾，可以伴隨猶豫或失落。區分認為應該發生什麼與自己的感受，也區分希望與已成結果。人物的態度不會自動屬於另一人物、敘述者或作者。保留對象、程度及限制，不脫離語境挑一個情緒詞。 背景：dramatist是劇作家，produce a play是籌辦演出，promise可以指潛力。composition是創作的作品，如歌曲，manuscript是文字稿，crude在此指粗糙。小說人物發言與回憶錄敘述者的反思是不同聲音，都不自動等於錄音朗讀者的意見。

workedExample.en: Unscored invented example: “I think the park should open earlier, although getting up for my shift will be hard. I hope we can try it next month,” says a caretaker. The caretaker supports the change while acknowledging a personal difficulty. This is neither complete opposition nor an announced successful trial; hope leaves the timing uncertain.
workedExample.zh-Hans: 不计分虚构示例：管理员说：“I think the park should open earlier, although getting up for my shift will be hard. I hope we can try it next month.” 管理员支持改变，也承认自己的困难；这既非完全反对，也非宣布试行成功，hope保留时间的不确定。
workedExample.zh-Hant: 不計分虛構示例：管理員說：「I think the park should open earlier, although getting up for my shift will be hard. I hope we can try it next month.」管理員支持改變，也承認自己的困難；這既非完全反對，也非宣布試行成功，hope保留時間的不確定。

questions.prompt: Which interpretation keeps the speaker’s attitude and its limits?
options: The narrator has the manuscripts before him now and remembers every line clearly. His criticism reports a current inspection of complete written copies rather than a hypothetical judgement.
The narrator regrets not writing down some compositions, despite thinking he would probably judge them crude if he had them now. Tentative criticism and a wish to have preserved them coexist.
The narrator is pleased he did not write the compositions down, because he now knows they have no value. His possible critical judgement cancels every reason to regret their loss.

explanations.zh-Hans: if I had…now是假设，only…a few lines限制了记得的内容；原文没有说现存手稿或完整记忆。
explanations.zh-Hant: if I had…now是假設，only…a few lines限制了記得的內容；原文沒有說現存手稿或完整記憶。
explanations.en: “If I had … now” is hypothetical, and “only … a few lines” limits what he recalls. The source does not describe existing manuscripts or perfect recall.

explanations.zh-Hans: I am sorry与only recall a few lines表达未记录下来的遗憾；Probably if I had…now…would让批评成为带保留的假设判断，并不抵消遗憾。回忆录上下文谈的是Barboza的歌，并不证明叙述者创作了它们；本题不要求从录音外辨认作者。
explanations.zh-Hant: I am sorry與only recall a few lines表達未記錄下來的遺憾；Probably if I had…now…would讓批評成為帶保留的假設判斷，並不抵消遺憾。回憶錄上下文談的是Barboza的歌，並不證明敘述者創作了它們；本題不要求從錄音外辨認作者。
explanations.en: “I am sorry” and “only recall a few lines” express regret over not recording them. “Probably if I had … now … would” makes the critical judgement hypothetical and qualified; it does not cancel that regret. The surrounding memoir concerns Barboza’s songs, not proof that the narrator composed them. The recording itself does not require identifying the composer.

explanations.zh-Hans: 叙述者明确遗憾没有保留；可能批评其质量与遗憾相容，并不证明作品毫无价值或他很庆幸。
explanations.zh-Hant: 敘述者明確遺憾沒有保留；可能批評其品質與遺憾相容，並不證明作品毫無價值或他很慶幸。
explanations.en: The narrator explicitly regrets not preserving them. A possible critical view of quality is compatible with regret; it does not establish that the works have no value or that he is pleased.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation keeps the speaker’s attitude and its limits?
options: The speaker is enthusiastic about the play’s potential while withholding its details. The speaker hopes to produce it within three months; neither that hope nor the praise guarantees the timetable or its success.
The speaker is dismissive of the play’s potential and refuses to produce it. Withholding its name and details shows that the speaker finds less promise in it than in other recent work.
The speaker announces guaranteed success and a fixed production deadline. That hope establishes that the play will certainly be produced within three months and outperform every other play.

explanations.zh-Hans: more promise…than anything…for months表达强烈看好，同时她仍保留姓名与细节。I hope限定三个月计划；保密不等于否定，乐观判断也不保证结果。原书场景是Elizabeth对记者说话，并非录音叙述者自己的制作计划。
explanations.zh-Hant: more promise…than anything…for months表達強烈看好，同時她仍保留姓名與細節。I hope限定三個月計劃；保密不等於否定，樂觀判斷也不保證結果。原書場景是Elizabeth對記者說話，並非錄音敘述者自己的製作計劃。
explanations.en: “More promise … than anything … for months” expresses strong positive expectation; she still withholds names and details. “I hope” qualifies the three-month plan. Confidentiality is not rejection, and an optimistic judgement is not a guaranteed outcome. The original scene identifies Elizabeth speaking to journalists; do not treat the fictional claim as the recording narrator’s own production plan.

explanations.zh-Hans: 这把明确的看好与制作意向颠倒了；不透露细节，不等于看衰或拒绝制作。
explanations.zh-Hant: 這把明確的看好與製作意向顛倒了；不透露細節，不等於看衰或拒絕製作。
explanations.en: This reverses the explicit praise and production intention. Withholding details does not mean she finds the work unpromising or refuses to produce it.

explanations.zh-Hans: 希望与认为有潜力都是带有限制的期待，并非确定时间表、测得的优越表现或必然成功。
explanations.zh-Hant: 希望與認為有潛力都是帶有限制的期待，並非確定時間表、測得的優越表現或必然成功。
explanations.en: Hope and perceived potential are qualified expectations, not a guaranteed schedule, measured superiority or certain success.

blocks.text: When a turtle is found stranded, it is impossible to know where it came from unless you retrace the path taken by its body since its death. When a sea turtle carcass floats, it drifts with currents and winds, just like a floating piece of plastic or wood would do, until it lands on the beach. Therefore, to predict this floating pathway, we must look at how the currents and winds transported the carcass as it floated on the sea surface. Other researchers had already made measurements to determine the effect of ocean currents on the trajectory of sea turtle carcasses. However, sea turtles have big shells that stick out of the water, meaning their movements are influenced by winds as well. No measurements had previously been taken regarding the effect of winds on sea turtle carcasses. We therefore conducted an experiment to determine the role played by winds in the trajectory of sea turtle carcasses.

materials.title: What Are the Small Lumps I See on Some Plant Roots?

credit.attribution: What Are the Small Lumps I See on Some Plant Roots? — Fede Berckx; Katharina Pawlowski. Frontiers for Young Minds. CC BY 4.0; complete original native paragraphs, whitespace normalised; media and third-party quotations excluded.

blocks.text: Although modern agriculture provides us with much of the food that we need, researchers have found that agriculture has a negative impact on our planet. The production of fertilizers releases greenhouse gasses, which enhance global warming. But at the same time, fertilizers help us to produce enough plants to satisfy the global demand for food, so we must balance the greenhouse gas emissions with the benefits that fertilizers provide to crops. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in plant nodules can help us because they provide nitrogen to plants and decrease the need for fertilizers. One way that farmers already make use of this symbiosis is to plant legumes in their fields in rotation with other crops. The legumes naturally increase the amount of nitrogen that is available in the soil. Some researchers are trying to modify the genes of crop plants so they have their own tools to fix nitrogen, without the need for bacteria. Other researchers are trying to understand why many plants lost the ability to form symbiotic relationships with bacteria and whether it is possible to re-introduce this ability into certain crop plants. By harnessing or improving the natural abilities of crop plants to obtain their own nutrients, hopefully we can decrease the negative impacts of agriculture on the environment and so many wild species while still growing enough food to feed the human population.

generator.scope: Client generation integrating facts, methods, aims, existing practice and qualifications on exact four inspected complete contexts; same-goal distinct-original application; complete raw source packages, no authored lessons or uninspected source approval.

teaching.en: First identify the information needed for the account, then connect it without changing its status. Keep observations, methods, existing practices, research aims and hoped-for outcomes distinct. A useful synthesis includes the relationships between facts, not just repeated words or an unordered list. Check every clause against the source: an accurate detail cannot rescue another invented clause. Preserve differences between groups and stages, along with words marking uncertainty or scope. Background: a carcass is a dead animal’s body; drift is movement carried by water or wind; trajectory is its path. A nodule is a small root structure. Nitrogen fixation makes nitrogen available for living systems; legumes include beans and peas; symbiosis is a close relationship between organisms. These terms support reading the account, not predicting a new experiment’s outcome.

questions.prompt: Which integrated account preserves the information and its status?
options: To retrace a dead turtle’s floating path, the account combines current and wind effects. Earlier measurements addressed currents; exposed shells make wind relevant, but its effect had not been measured. The described experiment addresses that gap, without reporting its measured results here.

To retrace a living turtle’s migration, the account uses measurements showing that wind alone determines the route. Earlier researchers had already measured wind effects, so the new experiment repeats a settled finding and rules out any role for currents.

To retrace a dead turtle’s floating path, earlier researchers had measured both current and wind effects. The paragraph reports the new experiment’s numerical results and proves that a stranded body’s beach location is necessarily the place where it died.

Current measurements were available; the shell’s exposure explains why the unmeasured wind effect matters. The final sentence states the experiment’s purpose, not its result. Stranding location is not automatically death location, and this is not live migration.

questions.prompt: Which integrated account preserves the information and its status?
options: The account treats fertilizer use as having only costs and no role in food production. It says legume rotation is merely an untested future idea, while all crop plants already fix their own nitrogen without bacteria and have no need for any symbiotic relationship.

The account treats legume rotation, direct plant nitrogen fixation and restored bacterial symbiosis as one method already achieved in every crop. Because they are identical, fertilizer production has stopped and the balance between food and emissions is guaranteed.

The account links food production with an emissions tradeoff. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria and existing legume rotation can reduce fertilizer needs. It distinguishes research on crops fixing nitrogen without bacteria from research on restoring plant–bacteria symbiosis; the hoped-for balance is not a completed universal solution.

explanations.zh-Hans: 这抹去产量益处，把已有做法挪到未来，又把仅属研究的直接固氮说成普遍事实。
explanations.zh-Hant: 這抹去產量益處，把已有做法挪到未來，又把僅屬研究的直接固氮說成普遍事實。
explanations.en: This deletes the food-production benefit, moves an existing practice into the future, and claims universal direct fixation that the paragraph presents only as research.

explanations.zh-Hans: 原文区分现行轮作与两条不同研究路径，没说它们相同或已普及，也没说停产肥料或保证平衡。
explanations.zh-Hant: 原文區分現行輪作與兩條不同研究路徑，沒說它們相同或已普及，也沒說停產肥料或保證平衡。
explanations.en: The text separates current rotation and two different research paths. They are not identical or completed in every crop, and no end to fertilizer production or guaranteed balance is stated.

explanations.zh-Hans: 本段同时保留肥料的产量益处与排放代价，点明轮作为现有做法，再区分不依赖细菌固氮与恢复共生两条研究方向。trying、whether、hopefully都阻止把研究写成普遍完成的结果。
explanations.zh-Hant: 本段同時保留肥料的產量益處與排放代價，點明輪作為現有做法，再區分不依賴細菌固氮與恢復共生兩條研究方向。trying、whether、hopefully都阻止把研究寫成普遍完成的結果。
explanations.en: The paragraph keeps fertilizer benefits and emissions together, names rotation as an existing use, then separates two research directions: independence from bacteria and renewed cooperation with them. “Trying”, “whether” and “hopefully” prevent turning those directions into a universal completed outcome.

blocks.text:
“A likely story indeed!” said the Pigeon in a tone of the deepest contempt. “I’ve seen a good many little girls in my time, but never _one_ with such a neck as that! No, no! You’re a serpent; and there’s no use denying it. I suppose you’ll be telling me next that you never tasted an egg!”

“I _have_ tasted eggs, certainly,” said Alice, who was a very truthful child; “but little girls eat eggs quite as much as serpents do, you know.”

“I don’t believe it,” said the Pigeon; “but if they do, why then they’re a kind of serpent, that’s all I can say.”

This was such a new idea to Alice, that she was quite silent for a minute or two, which gave the Pigeon the opportunity of adding, “You’re looking for eggs, I know _that_ well enough; and what does it matter to me whether you’re a little girl or a serpent?”

“It matters a good deal to _me_,” said Alice hastily; “but I’m not looking for eggs, as it happens; and if I was, I shouldn’t want _yours_: I don’t like them raw.”

“Well, be off, then!” said the Pigeon in a sulky tone, as it settled down again into its nest. Alice crouched down among the trees as well as she could, for her neck kept getting entangled among the branches, and every now and then she had to stop and untwist it. After a while she remembered that she still held the pieces of mushroom in her hands, and she set to work very carefully, nibbling first at one and then at the other, and growing sometimes taller and sometimes shorter, until she had succeeded in bringing herself down to her usual height.

blocks.text:
Anna: The city is exciting! It has more culture than the country. There are many museums and restaurants. Every night, there is theater and music. And, there are more jobs. That is why I'm here.

Phil: Well, I agree. There is more culture in the city and there might be more jobs. But the country has more nature! It's peaceful and beautiful. There are more trees and mountains. The air is clean. You can go hiking and camping. The city is not beautiful. It's noisy and dirty.

Anna: I disagree. I think all the different buildings are beautiful. And I like to watch all the different people.

Phil: That's another thing that is different. People in the country are friendly. They always say "hello!" Here, no one says "hello." I think city people are rude.

Anna: Well, I agree. Country people are friendly. But I don't think city people are rude. I think they're just busy.

Phil: That's a good point.

Anna: Look at me. I live in the city and I said "hello" to you.

Phil: But you are from the country.

Anna: I have an idea. Let's say "hello!" to people -- to many people!

blocks.text: Extreme halophilic and hyperthermophilic microbes were also included in Archaea. For a long time, archaea were seen as extremophiles that exist only in extreme habitats such as hot springs and salt lakes, but by the end of the 20th century, archaea had been identified in non-extreme environments as well. Today, they are known to be a large and diverse group of organisms abundantly distributed throughout nature. This new appreciation of the importance and ubiquity of archaea came from using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to detect prokaryotes from environmental samples (such as water or soil) by multiplying their ribosomal genes. This allows the detection and identification of organisms that have not been cultured in the laboratory.

blocks.text:
The nest is a platform of sticks in trees or shrubs. Unlike most other herons, it feeds in relatively dry grassy habitats, often accompanying cattle or other large mammals, since it catches insect and small vertebrate prey disturbed by these animals. Some populations of the Cattle Egret are migratory and others show post-breeding dispersal.

The adult Cattle Egret has few predators, but birds or mammals may raid its nests, and chicks may be lost to starvation, calcium deficiency or disturbance from other large birds. This species removes ticks and flies from cattle, but it can be a safety hazard at airfields, and has been implicated in the spread of tick-borne animal diseases.

teaching.en: First identify the information needed for the account, then connect it without changing its status. Keep observations, methods, existing practices, research aims and hoped-for outcomes distinct. A useful synthesis includes the relationships between facts, not just repeated words or an unordered list. Check every clause against the source: an accurate detail cannot rescue another invented clause. Preserve differences between groups and stages, along with words marking uncertainty or scope. Background: archaea are microorganisms; halophilic concerns salty conditions and hyperthermophilic very hot conditions. PCR copies genetic material for detection; cultured means grown in a laboratory. Ribosomal genes are the genetic targets named here. A cattle egret is a bird; prey is food it catches; dispersal means spreading away; ticks are small parasites; airfields are places where aircraft operate. Interpret these recorded versions, without needing current taxonomy or wildlife-management advice.

questions.prompt: Which integrated account preserves the information and its status?
options: The account revises an extreme-habitat-only view after archaea were identified in non-extreme settings too. It connects that broader understanding with PCR detection of genes in environmental samples, including organisms not cultured in a laboratory; the method reveals distribution rather than causing organisms to move.

The account confirms that archaea exist only in hot springs and salt lakes. PCR first grew all the organisms in laboratory cultures, and those cultures were then moved outdoors, creating the new non-extreme populations described in the account.

The account says archaea left extreme habitats entirely and can now all survive in every environment. The new view arose without environmental sampling or genetic detection, so the discussion of PCR has no connection to the change in understanding.

explanations.zh-Hans: 新的分布范围扩展了早先看法；材料把这种认识与环境样本的基因检测相连，并明确包括未在实验室培养的生物。检测基因不等于培养或搬迁生物，分布多样也不等于每种都能活在任何地方。这里解释录制版本，today不作当前分类学更新。
explanations.zh-Hant: 新的分布範圍擴展了早先看法；材料把這種認識與環境樣本的基因檢測相連，並明確包括未在實驗室培養的生物。檢測基因不等於培養或搬遷生物，分布多樣也不等於每種都能活在任何地方。這裡解釋錄製版本，today不作當前分類學更新。
explanations.en: The habitat range broadens the earlier view; the account links this understanding to gene detection from environmental samples and explicitly includes uncultured organisms. Detecting genes is not growing every organism or relocating it, and diverse distribution does not mean every organism survives everywhere. Interpret this recorded account rather than treating its “today” as a current taxonomy update.

explanations.zh-Hans: 这保留了被扩展的“仅极端环境”看法，并编造培养与搬迁过程；录音说PCR可识别未培养的生物。
explanations.zh-Hant: 這保留了被擴展的「僅極端環境」看法，並編造培養與搬遷過程；錄音說PCR可識別未培養的生物。
explanations.en: This preserves the rejected only-extreme view and invents culturing and relocation. The recording says PCR can identify organisms that have not been cultured.

explanations.zh-Hans: 增加非极端环境，不是全部取代极端环境。录音明确把新认识与环境PCR检测相连，也没说所有生物处处可活。
explanations.zh-Hant: 增加非極端環境，不是全部取代極端環境。錄音明確把新認識與環境PCR檢測相連，也沒說所有生物處處可活。
explanations.en: Non-extreme habitats are added, not substituted for all extreme habitats. The recording explicitly connects the new appreciation with environmental PCR detection; it makes no all-organisms/everywhere claim.

questions.prompt: Which integrated account preserves the information and its status?
options: The account says all populations follow the same migration pattern and feed chiefly in deep water. Because adults have few predators, nests and chicks face no threats; removing ticks proves the birds cannot create any hazards for aircraft or other animals.

The account links feeding near cattle only with harm and denies that the birds catch disturbed prey or remove parasites. It says every adult faces the same threats as every chick and that the listed airfield risk replaces, rather than coexists with, any beneficial role.

The account links dry-grass feeding with prey disturbed by large mammals, while movement varies between populations. Few adult predators do not remove nest and chick risks. Removing cattle parasites can coexist with airfield and disease hazards, so the bird is neither uniformly risk-free nor purely harmful.

explanations.zh-Hans: 这抹去种群差异，改掉较干燥的生境，把成鸟天敌少扩大成巢／幼鸟无风险，还删去了机场与疾病限制。
explanations.zh-Hant: 這抹去種群差異，改掉較乾燥的生境，把成鳥天敵少擴大成巢／幼鳥無風險，還刪去了機場與疾病限制。
explanations.en: This erases population differences, changes the stated dry habitat and extends few adult predators to no nest/chick risk. It also deletes the explicit airfield and disease qualifications.

explanations.zh-Hans: 原文明说了惊起猎物与除寄生虫，区分成鸟和幼鸟风险；危害与益处并存，而非取消益处。
explanations.zh-Hant: 原文明說了驚起獵物與除寄生蟲，區分成鳥和幼鳥風險；危害與益處並存，而非取消益處。
explanations.en: The account explicitly explains disturbed prey and parasite removal. Adult and chick risks are distinguished, and the hazards accompany rather than cancel the beneficial role.

explanations.zh-Hans: 须同时保留四点：哺乳动物惊起猎物解释伴随觅食，种群移动方式有别，成鸟被捕食与巢／幼鸟风险不同，除寄生虫的益处又与特定危害并存。这些限制不支持一概有益或一概有害。本题解释录制的物种描述，并非当前野生动物管理建议。
explanations.zh-Hant: 須同時保留四點：哺乳動物驚起獵物解釋伴隨覓食，種群移動方式有別，成鳥被捕食與巢／幼鳥風險不同，除寄生蟲的益處又與特定危害並存。這些限制不支持一概有益或一概有害。本題解釋錄製的物種描述，並非當前野生動物管理建議。
explanations.en: Four parts must remain together: disturbed prey explains feeding with mammals; populations differ in movement; adult predation differs from nest/chick risks; and parasite removal coexists with specified hazards. The qualifications do not support a single all-benefit or all-harm label. The task interprets the recorded species account, not a current wildlife-management recommendation.

materials.title: Specialization of Functions in the Human Brain

credit.attribution: Specialization of Functions in the Human Brain — Josef Parvizi. Frontiers for Young Minds. CC BY 4.0; complete original native paragraphs, whitespace normalised; media and third-party quotations excluded.
credit.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Article-specific original grant; images, quoted third-party text and excluded material omitted.

blocks.text: Once the idea of fluid-filled brain chambers was ridiculed, one had to find other ways to explain how the human brain works. An Austrian scientist called Franz Joseph Gall promoted the idea that there are specific centers in the brain for specific functions [3]. This idea, known as phrenology, argued that if you use a part of your brain frequently, you become very good at it, and that particular brain area grows in size and creates a little bump in the skull bone. Let's say we have a math center in the brain. If you use math all the time, you become very good at it. You may become like Einstein. If that happens, your math center in the brain has grown a lot. If I study your skull bone, I should see a little bump over your head right over the math center. The same thing holds for brain centers for love, sex, emotions, language, etc. So if you study the bumps in the skull bone, you will be able to guess what that person is good at. You can call this crazy idea, “bumpology”! In fact, a lot of offices were specialized in studying bumps in heads and describing people's characters. If you wanted to marry someone, you could take your girlfriend or boyfriend to one of those offices and ask the “bumpologist” to predict if your bumps are compatible with the bumps of your partner-to-be.

materials.title: Birds and Their Extraordinary Sense of Smell

credit.attribution: Birds and Their Extraordinary Sense of Smell — Renee Li; Nivritti Mantha; Ichie Ojiro; Hiroaki Matsunami; Robert Driver. Frontiers for Young Minds. CC BY 4.0; complete original native paragraphs, whitespace normalised; media and third-party quotations excluded.
credit.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Article-specific original grant; images, quoted third-party text and excluded material omitted.

blocks.text: For a long time, it was thought that most birds could not smell many odors [4]. After all, birds are colorful, are often active during daylight hours, and some species sing beautiful songs. Therefore, people thought that birds do not use smell but instead have better vision and hearing. Early experiments on bird behavior agreed with this idea. For example, the famous ornithologist John James Audubon conducted an experiment on turkey vultures and concluded they could not smell meat. Increasingly though, we are learning the opposite: birds may use smell. For example, finches preferred the smell of their own egg instead of the egg of another finch, hinting that birds may use smell to recognize family members [5]. Similarly, other birds showed a preference for vanilla-scented nesting materials, showing that birds may use smell as a guide when building nests [6]. When scientists placed food for albatrosses in the ocean, the albatrosses successfully navigated many miles across the ocean directly to the source of the food, suggesting that birds use smell while foraging [7]. Why did Audubon’s vultures seem to not be able to smell, then? The meat Audubon used may have been too rotten to be appealing to the vultures.

teaching.en: Ask who says, thinks or questions each claim, then keep that person’s view separate from the writer’s commitment. A report of a claim is not proof that it is true. A writer may discuss an older proposal, offer a hypothetical illustration, or describe a character considering alternatives without endorsing them. Preserve reporting verbs and uncertainty; agreement to proceed or accept a description need not be a genuine belief. Distinguish the person holding a view from the person receiving a report or being discussed. Background: an ornithologist studies birds; vultures feed on carrion, or dead animals; foraging is looking for food. Phrenology names a historical proposal about skull shape and mental traits. A hypothetical example illustrates an idea rather than reporting an actual study. Names in an analogy are not automatically sources of the proposal.

blocks.text: Freud’s ideas were influential, and you will learn more about them when you study lifespan development, personality, and therapy. For instance, many therapists believe strongly in the unconscious and the impact of early childhood experiences on the rest of a person’s life. The method of psychoanalysis, which involves the patient talking about their experiences and selves, while not invented by Freud, was certainly popularized by him and is still used today. Many of Freud’s other ideas, however, are controversial. Drew Westen (1998) argues that many of the criticisms of Freud’s ideas are misplaced, in that they attack his older ideas without taking into account later writings. Westen also argues that critics fail to consider the success of the broad ideas that Freud introduced or developed, such as the importance of childhood experiences in adult motivations, the role of unconscious versus conscious motivations in driving our behavior, the fact that motivations can cause conflicts that affect behavior, the effects of mental representations of ourselves and others in guiding our interactions, and the development of personality over time. Westen identifies subsequent research support for all of these ideas.

blocks.text:
Dr Halpin, assistant house surgeon of the City of Dublin Hospital, stated that the deceased had two lower ribs fractured and had sustained severe contusions of the right shoulder. The right side of the head had been injured in the fall. The injuries were not sufficient to have caused death in a normal person. Death, in his opinion, had been probably due to shock and sudden failure of the heart’s action.

Mr H. B. Patterson Finlay, on behalf of the railway company, expressed his deep regret at the accident. The company had always taken every precaution to prevent people crossing the lines except by the bridges, both by placing notices in every station and by the use of patent spring gates at level crossings. The deceased had been in the habit of crossing the lines late at night from platform to platform and, in view of certain other circumstances of the case, he did not think the railway officials were to blame.

Captain Sinico, of Leoville, Sydney Parade, husband of the deceased, also gave evidence. He stated that the deceased was his wife. He was not in Dublin at the time of the accident as he had arrived only that morning from Rotterdam. They had been married for twenty-two years and had lived happily until about two years ago when his wife began to be rather intemperate in her habits.

Miss Mary Sinico said that of late her mother had been in the habit of going out at night to buy spirits. She, witness, had often tried to reason with her mother and had induced her to join a league. She was not at home until an hour after the accident. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence and exonerated Lennon from all blame.

exactEvidence:
Dr Halpin, assistant house surgeon of the City of Dublin Hospital, stated that the deceased had two lower ribs fractured and had sustained severe contusions of the right shoulder. The right side of the head had been injured in the fall. The injuries were not sufficient to have caused death in a normal person. Death, in his opinion, had been probably due to shock and sudden failure of the heart’s action.

Mr H. B. Patterson Finlay, on behalf of the railway company, expressed his deep regret at the accident. The company had always taken every precaution to prevent people crossing the lines except by the bridges, both by placing notices in every station and by the use of patent spring gates at level crossings. The deceased had been in the habit of crossing the lines late at night from platform to platform and, in view of certain other circumstances of the case, he did not think the railway officials were to blame.

Captain Sinico, of Leoville, Sydney Parade, husband of the deceased, also gave evidence. He stated that the deceased was his wife. He was not in Dublin at the time of the accident as he had arrived only that morning from Rotterdam. They had been married for twenty-two years and had lived happily until about two years ago when his wife began to be rather intemperate in her habits.

Miss Mary Sinico said that of late her mother had been in the habit of going out at night to buy spirits. She, witness, had often tried to reason with her mother and had induced her to join a league. She was not at home until an hour after the accident. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence and exonerated Lennon from all blame.

teaching.en: Ask who says, thinks or questions each claim, then keep that person’s view separate from the writer’s commitment. A report of a claim is not proof that it is true. A writer may discuss an older proposal, offer a hypothetical illustration, or describe a character considering alternatives without endorsing them. Preserve reporting verbs and uncertainty; agreement to proceed or accept a description need not be a genuine belief. Distinguish the person holding a view from the person receiving a report or being discussed. Background: effects can mean personal belongings; a suite can be a set of offices; deny means say something is not so. Blotting-paper absorbs ink; a lawyer advises on legal matters; probe can mean try to discover a view. One account concerns historical office reports, the other fictional deliberation. The task attributes what is said or considered; it does not decide a legal dispute or a person’s true identity.
teaching.zh-Hans: 逐项问是谁在说、想或质疑，再区分那个人的观点与作者认可的内容。转述主张，不等于证明主张真实。作者可能讨论旧提议、作假设示例，或叙述人物考虑几种可能，而没有表示认可。保留报告动词和不确定性；同意继续或接受一种说法，不一定是真心相信。还要区分持观点者、报告接收者及被讨论者。 背景：effects可以指个人物品，suite可以是一组办公室，deny是否认；blotting-paper吸墨，lawyer是律师，probe可以指试探想法。一份材料是历史办公室报告，另一份是小说人物思考。本题归属发言或推测，并不裁定法律争议或人物真实身份。
teaching.zh-Hant: 逐項問是誰在說、想或質疑，再區分那個人的觀點與作者認可的內容。轉述主張，不等於證明主張真實。作者可能討論舊提議、作假設示例，或敘述人物考慮幾種可能，而沒有表示認可。保留報告動詞和不確定性；同意繼續或接受一種說法，不一定是真心相信。還要區分持觀點者、報告接收者及被討論者。 背景：effects可以指個人物品，suite可以是一組辦公室，deny是否認；blotting-paper吸墨，lawyer是律師，probe可以指試探想法。一份材料是歷史辦公室報告，另一份是小說人物思考。本題歸屬發言或推測，並不裁定法律爭議或人物真實身分。

workedExample.en: Unscored invented example: A reporter writes, “Iris says the bridge is closed. Leon says Iris has not checked its gate. I cannot confirm which account is right.” Iris holds the closure claim; Leon questions her checking; the reporter withholds a verdict. This does not make Leon the source of the closure claim or prove the bridge is open.

questions.prompt: Which account keeps each reported view with its source and preserves what is uncertain?
options: Gray says Gandy looked through files and approved his work, while Gandy denies looking. Nixon is identified as the person who gave Gandy the one-week estimate and personally secured the office.

The narrator confirms that Gandy and Gray agreed he looked through the files. Because Gray reported securing the office, the recording establishes that all files in the entire suite were secured and contains no conflicting account.

Gandy says Gray looked through files and approved her work; Gray denies looking. The further secured-office statement is Gray’s report to Nixon. Keeping these reports separate does not decide whether Gray looked or establish that every file was actually secured.

explanations.zh-Hans: 这颠倒报告角色，把Nixon从接收者改成行动者；录音把批准与时间估计分别放在Gandy的说法中。

explanations.en: The reporting roles are reversed and Nixon is turned from recipient into actor. The recording attributes approval and the time estimate to Gandy’s statements.

explanations.zh-Hans: 否认明确与Gandy的说法冲突；报告“办公室已保全”，不等于叙述者证实所有文件或整个办公套间均已保全。
explanations.zh-Hant: 否認明確與Gandy的說法衝突；報告「辦公室已保全」，不等於敘述者證實所有文件或整個辦公套間均已保全。
explanations.en: The denial explicitly conflicts with Gandy’s account. A reported secured-office claim is not narrator-confirmed proof about all files or the whole suite.

explanations.zh-Hans: Gandy stated把查看／批准归给她的说法，Gray was to deny把否认归给Gray；Gray reported to Nixon是另一次报告，Nixon是接收者。报告动词不裁定查看争议，也不证明保全了多少东西。一周的说法同样来自Gandy，并非Nixon。
explanations.zh-Hant: Gandy stated把查看／批准歸給她的說法，Gray was to deny把否認歸給Gray；Gray reported to Nixon是另一次報告，Nixon是接收者。報告動詞不裁定查看爭議，也不證明保全了多少東西。一週的說法同樣來自Gandy，並非Nixon。
explanations.en: “Gandy stated” assigns looking/approval to her account; “Gray was to deny” assigns the denial to him. “Gray reported to Nixon” introduces another report, with Nixon as recipient. These reporting verbs do not adjudicate the looking dispute or prove the extent secured. The one-week statement is also Gandy’s, not Nixon’s.

questions.prompt: Which account keeps each reported view with its source and preserves what is uncertain?
options: The narrator confirms that Julius genuinely believes the identity and rules out any attempt to probe Durham’s view. Durham simply repeats that established fact, so the passage contains no unresolved alternative about Julius’s motive.

The narrator reports Durham considering two possibilities about Julius: genuine belief in the identity, or an attempt to discover Durham’s view. Those alternatives are Durham’s uncertainty, not Julius’s confirmed thoughts. Durham’s later acceptance is a decision, not proof of Julius’s actual belief.

Julius is the person wondering whether Durham believes the identity or is probing him. The later acceptance is Julius’s decision, and the narrator attributes neither the uncertainty nor the decision to Durham.

explanations.zh-Hans: 原文用if／or保留两种可能，没有把它们定成叙述者确认的Julius信念；后来的决定本身不能消除该不确定性。
explanations.zh-Hant: 原文用if／or保留兩種可能，沒有把它們定成敘述者確認的Julius信念；後來的決定本身不能消除該不確定性。
explanations.en: The text preserves two possible explanations through if/or; it does not resolve them into a narrator-confirmed Julius belief. A later decision cannot by itself erase that uncertainty.

explanations.zh-Hans: He wondered前的主体是Durham，he—Durham又明确指出Julius可能在探哪一个人的想法。if／or两种可能属于Durham的思考。律师后来的决定本身不解决Julius实际相信什么。本题不问真实身份，也不把谈话中的接受等同于真心相信。
explanations.zh-Hant: He wondered前的主體是Durham，he—Durham又明確指出Julius可能在探哪一個人的想法。if／or兩種可能屬於Durham的思考。律師後來的決定本身不解決Julius實際相信什麼。本題不問真實身分，也不把談話中的接受等同於真心相信。
explanations.en: Durham is the subject before “He wondered”; “he—Durham” explicitly identifies whose view Julius might be probing. The if/or alternatives belong to Durham’s deliberation. The lawyer’s later decision does not itself resolve what Julius actually believes. This question does not ask the person’s true identity or equate conversational acceptance with genuine belief.

explanations.zh-Hans: 这交换了思考者与被揣测者；疑问和律师的决定都在叙述Durham，并非Julius。
explanations.zh-Hant: 這交換了思考者與被揣測者；疑問和律師的決定都在敘述Durham，並非Julius。
explanations.en: This swaps the thinker and the person being considered. Both the wondering and the lawyer’s decision are narrated about Durham, not Julius.

“I am disposed to be gregarious and communicative to-night,” he repeated, “and that is why I sent for you: the fire and the chandelier were not sufficient company for me; nor would Pilot have been, for none of these can talk. Adèle is a degree better, but still far below the mark; Mrs. Fairfax ditto; you, I am persuaded, can suit me if you will: you puzzled me the first evening I invited you down here. I have almost forgotten you since: other ideas have driven yours from my head; but to-night I am resolved to be at ease; to dismiss what importunes, and recall what pleases. It would please me now to draw you out—to learn more of you—therefore speak.”

Instead of speaking, I smiled; and not a very complacent or submissive smile either.

“Speak,” he urged.

“What about, sir?”

“Whatever you like. I leave both the choice of subject and the manner of treating it entirely to yourself.”

Accordingly I sat and said nothing: “If he expects me to talk for the mere sake of talking and showing off, he will find he has addressed himself to the wrong person,” I thought.

“You are dumb, Miss Eyre.”

I was dumb still. He bent his head a little towards me, and with a single hasty glance seemed to dive into my eyes.

“Stubborn?” he said, “and annoyed. Ah! it is consistent. I put my request in an absurd, almost insolent form. Miss Eyre, I beg your pardon. The fact is, once for all, I don’t wish to treat you like an inferior: that is” (correcting himself), “I claim only such superiority as must result from twenty years’ difference in age and a century’s advance in experience. This is legitimate, _et j’y tiens_, as Adèle would say; and it is by virtue of this superiority, and this alone, that I desire you to have the goodness to talk to me a little now, and divert my thoughts, which are galled with dwelling on one point—cankering as a rusty nail.”

He had deigned an explanation, almost an apology, and I did not feel insensible to his condescension, and would not seem so.

“I am willing to amuse you, if I can, sir—quite willing; but I cannot introduce a topic, because how do I know what will interest you? Ask me questions, and I will do my best to answer them.”

“Then, in the first place, do you agree with me that I have a right to be a little masterful, abrupt, perhaps exacting, sometimes, on the grounds I stated, namely, that I am old enough to be your father, and that I have battled through a varied experience with many men of many nations, and roamed over half the globe, while you have lived quietly with one set of people in one house?”

“Do as you please, sir.”

“That is no answer; or rather it is a very irritating, because a very evasive one. Reply clearly.”

“I don’t think, sir, you have a right to command me, merely because you are older than I, or because you have seen more of the world than I have; your claim to superiority depends on the use you have made of your time and experience.”

“Humph! Promptly spoken. But I won’t allow that, seeing that it would never suit my case, as I have made an indifferent, not to say a bad, use of both advantages. Leaving superiority out of the question, then, you must still agree to receive my orders now and then, without being piqued or hurt by the tone of command. Will you?”

I smiled: I thought to myself Mr. Rochester _is_ peculiar—he seems to forget that he pays me £30 per annum for receiving his orders.

“The smile is very well,” said he, catching instantly the passing expression; “but speak too.”

“I was thinking, sir, that very few masters would trouble themselves to inquire whether or not their paid subordinates were piqued and hurt by their orders.”

“Paid subordinates! What! you are my paid subordinate, are you? Oh yes, I had forgotten the salary! Well then, on that mercenary ground, will you agree to let me hector a little?”

“No, sir, not on that ground; but, on the ground that you did forget it, and that you care whether or not a dependent is comfortable in his dependency, I agree heartily.”

“And will you consent to dispense with a great many conventional forms and phrases, without thinking that the omission arises from insolence?”

“I am sure, sir, I should never mistake informality for insolence: one I rather like, the other nothing free-born would submit to, even for a salary.”

When I came home to West Egg that night I was afraid for a moment that my house was on fire. Two o’clock and the whole corner of the peninsula was blazing with light, which fell unreal on the shrubbery and made thin elongating glints upon the roadside wires. Turning a corner, I saw that it was Gatsby’s house, lit from tower to cellar.

At first I thought it was another party, a wild rout that had resolved itself into “hide-and-go-seek” or “sardines-in-the-box” with all the house thrown open to the game. But there wasn’t a sound. Only wind in the trees, which blew the wires and made the lights go off and on again as if the house had winked into the darkness. As my taxi groaned away I saw Gatsby walking toward me across his lawn.

“Your place looks like the World’s Fair,” I said.

“Does it?” He turned his eyes toward it absently. “I have been glancing into some of the rooms. Let’s go to Coney Island, old sport. In my car.”

“It’s too late.”

“Well, suppose we take a plunge in the swimming pool? I haven’t made use of it all summer.”

“I’ve got to go to bed.”

“All right.”

He waited, looking at me with suppressed eagerness.

“I talked with Miss Baker,” I said after a moment. “I’m going to call up Daisy tomorrow and invite her over here to tea.”

“Oh, that’s all right,” he said carelessly. “I don’t want to put you to any trouble.”

“What day would suit you?”

“What day would suit you?” he corrected me quickly. “I don’t want to put you to any trouble, you see.”

“How about the day after tomorrow?”

He considered for a moment. Then, with reluctance: “I want to get the grass cut,” he said.

We both looked down at the grass—there was a sharp line where my ragged lawn ended and the darker, well-kept expanse of his began. I suspected that he meant my grass.

“There’s another little thing,” he said uncertainly, and hesitated.

“Would you rather put it off for a few days?” I asked.

“Oh, it isn’t about that. At least—” He fumbled with a series of beginnings. “Why, I thought—why, look here, old sport, you don’t make much money, do you?”

“Not very much.”

This seemed to reassure him and he continued more confidently.

“I thought you didn’t, if you’ll pardon my—you see, I carry on a little business on the side, a sort of side line, you understand. And I thought that if you don’t make very much—You’re selling bonds, aren’t you, old sport?”

“Trying to.”

“Well, this would interest you. It wouldn’t take up much of your time and you might pick up a nice bit of money. It happens to be a rather confidential sort of thing.”

I realize now that under different circumstances that conversation might have been one of the crises of my life. But, because the offer was obviously and tactlessly for a service to be rendered, I had no choice except to cut him off there.

“I’ve got my hands full,” I said. “I’m much obliged but I couldn’t take on any more work.”

“You wouldn’t have to do any business with Wolfshiem.” Evidently he thought that I was shying away from the “gonnegtion” mentioned at lunch, but I assured him he was wrong. He waited a moment longer, hoping I’d begin a conversation, but I was too absorbed to be responsive, so he went unwillingly home.

The evening had made me lightheaded and happy; I think I walked into a deep sleep as I entered my front door. So I don’t know whether or not Gatsby went to Coney Island, or for how many hours he “glanced into rooms” while his house blazed gaudily on. I called up Daisy from the office next morning, and invited her to come to tea.

“Don’t bring Tom,” I warned her.

“What?”

“Don’t bring Tom.”

“Who is ‘Tom’?” she asked innocently.

The day agreed upon was pouring rain. At eleven o’clock a man in a raincoat, dragging a lawn-mower, tapped at my front door and said that Mr. Gatsby had sent him over to cut my grass. This reminded me that I had forgotten to tell my Finn to come back, so I drove into West Egg Village to search for her among soggy whitewashed alleys and to buy some cups and lemons and flowers.

generator.scope: Exact inspected complete native exchanges or source-bound original recording contexts. Same communicative-purpose goal across two distinct originals; no authored lesson bank, general uninspected context approval or CEFR calibration.

teaching.en: Read the whole exchange before assigning an intention. First identify what was asked or offered and what the response literally says. Then compare the response with the next turn and any stated private thought: an excuse can decline without voicing the objection, and apparent permission can evade endorsement. Distinguish the responder’s evidenced purpose from the other person’s interpretation. Choose the account supported by several turns; do not invent a secret motive or treat politeness as automatic agreement. Background: Nick narrates an encounter with Gatsby about inviting Daisy to tea; Wolfshiem is a previously mentioned business contact. Jane narrates a conversation with her employer Rochester. “Hands full” means busy, “gonnegtion” is the source’s spelling of connection, “hector” means bully, and “insolence” means disrespect. These historical power relations are represented, not endorsed.
teaching.zh-Hans: 先通读交流，再判断意图。先辨明对方问了或提议什么、答复字面说了什么；再与下一轮及明确写出的内心想法比较：借口可能在不直说顾虑的情况下拒绝，表面允许也可能回避认可。区分答复者有证据的用意与对方的理解，选择多个话轮支持的解释；不编造秘密动机，也不把礼貌自动当作同意。背景：Nick叙述与Gatsby商量邀请Daisy喝茶，Wolfshiem是之前提过的业务联系人；Jane叙述与雇主Rochester的谈话。hands full指忙，gonnegtion是原文对connection的写法，hector指欺凌，insolence指无礼。材料呈现历史权力关系，并非认可它们。

workedExample.en: Unscored invented example: “Will you chair the meeting?” asks Arun. Mei thinks she dislikes how the agenda was imposed, but says, “My calendar is rather full.” Arun offers a later date. Mei replies, “Thank you, but please ask someone else.” The first answer indirectly declines while withholding the agenda objection; Arun initially hears a scheduling problem. The final refusal rules out accepting a later slot. It does not prove that Mei’s calendar was empty.
workedExample.zh-Hans: 不计分虚构示例：Arun问：“Will you chair the meeting?” Mei心想自己不喜欢被强加的议程，却说：“My calendar is rather full.” Arun提议改期。Mei回答：“Thank you, but please ask someone else.” 第一次答复间接拒绝，同时没有说出议程方面的顾虑；Arun起初理解成时间问题。最后的拒绝排除了接受改期，但不能证明Mei的日程原本空闲。
workedExample.zh-Hant: 不計分虛構示例：Arun問：「Will you chair the meeting?」Mei心想自己不喜歡被強加的議程，卻說：「My calendar is rather full.」Arun提議改期。Mei回答：「Thank you, but please ask someone else.」第一次答覆間接拒絕，同時沒有說出議程方面的顧慮；Arun起初理解成時間問題。最後的拒絕排除了接受改期，但不能證明Mei的日程原本空閒。

questions.prompt: Which interpretation distinguishes the apparent message from its supported communicative purpose and the audience’s understanding?
options: Jane’s apparently permissive reply avoids directly endorsing Rochester’s claimed right to command. He presses for a clear answer, and she then disputes age or experience alone as sufficient authority. Her later acceptance of informality still excludes insolence, so it is not unrestricted submission.

Jane freely grants Rochester unlimited authority because he is older and pays her. His demand for clarity confirms her agreement, and her later distinction between informality and insolence withdraws every boundary on his conduct.

Jane’s reply refuses all conversation and every informal interaction with Rochester. Her next answer treats age and travel as sufficient authority, but her final answer rejects informality itself rather than distinguishing it from insolence.

explanations.zh-Hans: 下一轮把答复称为回避，Jane随后明确拒绝了字面上似乎授予的资格。她后来允许不拘礼节，但给无礼划出边界。功能须跨话轮理解，不能归纳成这句话永远表示拒绝。
explanations.zh-Hant: 下一輪把答覆稱為迴避，Jane隨後明確拒絕了字面上似乎授予的資格。她後來允許不拘禮節，但給無禮劃出邊界。功能須跨話輪理解，不能歸納成這句話永遠表示拒絕。
explanations.en: The next turn calls the reply evasive, and Jane’s explicit answer withholds the entitlement the literal words might seem to grant. She later permits informality while drawing a firm boundary at insolence. The function is understood across turns; it is not a rule that this phrase always means refusal.

explanations.zh-Hans: 回避并非明确同意。Jane明确否认仅凭年龄或见识就有权命令，又区分可以接受的不拘礼节和即使付薪也不能接受的无礼。
explanations.zh-Hant: 迴避並非明確同意。Jane明確否認僅憑年齡或見識就有權命令，又區分可以接受的不拘禮節和即使付薪也不能接受的無禮。
explanations.en: An evasive answer is not clear agreement. Jane explicitly rejects age or worldly experience alone as a right to command and distinguishes accepted informality from unacceptable insolence, even for pay.

explanations.zh-Hans: Jane愿意回答问题，也说自己喜欢不拘礼节。她质疑的是对方提出的权力根据，既未认可它，也未拒绝一切交谈；这个选项颠倒了两处限定。
explanations.zh-Hant: Jane願意回答問題，也說自己喜歡不拘禮節。她質疑的是對方提出的權力根據，既未認可它，也未拒絕一切交談；這個選項顛倒了兩處限定。
explanations.en: Jane offers to answer questions and says she likes informality. She challenges the proposed basis of authority; she does not endorse it or reject all conversation. The alternative reverses both qualifications.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation distinguishes the apparent message from its supported communicative purpose and the audience’s understanding?
options: Nick accepts the business offer but delays it until he finishes arranging the tea. His expression of thanks commits him to work with Wolfshiem, and Gatsby correctly understands this as a request for a higher payment.

Nick’s workload is established as his sole objection, with no social implication. Both men explicitly agree that the tea is a paid service, and Gatsby’s mention of Wolfshiem confirms that he understands Nick’s actual reason.

Nick presents his refusal as lack of time, avoiding a direct accusation that the business offer would pay for arranging the tea. His narration supplies that objection; Gatsby instead suspects reluctance about Wolfshiem, so the polite refusal has not made Nick’s reason explicit to him.

explanations.zh-Hans: 感谢之后明确说不能再接工作，并未接受。叙述否认了Gatsby关于Wolfshiem的理解，也没有要求更高酬金。
explanations.zh-Hant: 感謝之後明確說不能再接工作，並未接受。敘述否認了Gatsby關於Wolfshiem的理解，也沒有要求更高酬金。
explanations.en: Thanks accompanies an explicit inability to take on work; it does not accept the offer. The narrator rejects Gatsby’s Wolfshiem interpretation. Nothing requests a higher fee.

explanations.zh-Hans: 内心叙述给出的顾虑不同于口头借口，Gatsby的理解也被明确纠正。只按工作量的字面说法解释，会抹去这段对话中的误解。
explanations.zh-Hant: 內心敘述給出的顧慮不同於口頭藉口，Gatsby的理解也被明確糾正。只按工作量的字面說法解釋，會抹去這段對話中的誤解。
explanations.en: The private narration gives a different objection from the public excuse, and Gatsby’s interpretation is explicitly corrected. Treating the literal workload claim as the whole intention erases the exchange’s misunderstanding.

explanations.zh-Hans: 叙述指出Nick认为这是对帮忙的酬付，口头答复却以工作太多婉拒。下一轮显示Gatsby把障碍理解成另一件事。因此这里是间接拒绝，不是接受、议价或双方已明白同一原因；材料并未核实Nick实际有多少工作。
explanations.zh-Hant: 敘述指出Nick認為這是對幫忙的酬付，口頭答覆卻以工作太多婉拒。下一輪顯示Gatsby把障礙理解成另一件事。因此這裡是間接拒絕，不是接受、議價或雙方已明白同一原因；材料並未核實Nick實際有多少工作。
explanations.en: The narration identifies the perceived payment-for-service problem; the spoken reply gives a workload excuse. The next turn shows Gatsby construing the obstacle differently. This supports an indirect refusal, not acceptance, a fee negotiation or shared understanding. It does not establish what Nick’s workload actually was.

blocks.text:
Jo couldn’t help smiling at the important air which Meg had unconsciously assumed and which was as becoming as the pretty color varying in her cheeks.

“Would you mind telling me what you’d say?” asked Jo more respectfully.

“Not at all. You are sixteen now, quite old enough to be my confidant, and my experience will be useful to you by-and-by, perhaps, in your own affairs of this sort.”

“Don’t mean to have any. It’s fun to watch other people philander, but I should feel like a fool doing it myself,” said Jo, looking alarmed at the thought.

“I think not, if you liked anyone very much, and he liked you.” Meg spoke as if to herself, and glanced out at the lane where she had often seen lovers walking together in the summer twilight.

“I thought you were going to tell your speech to that man,” said Jo, rudely shortening her sister’s little reverie.

“Oh, I should merely say, quite calmly and decidedly, ‘Thank you, Mr. Brooke, you are very kind, but I agree with Father that I am too young to enter into any engagement at present, so please say no more, but let us be friends as we were.’”

“Hum, that’s stiff and cool enough! I don’t believe you’ll ever say it, and I know he won’t be satisfied if you do. If he goes on like the rejected lovers in books, you’ll give in, rather than hurt his feelings.”

blocks.text:
“It’s no use, John Clay,” said Holmes blandly. “You have no chance at all.”

“So I see,” the other answered with the utmost coolness. “I fancy that my pal is all right, though I see you have got his coat-tails.”

“There are three men waiting for him at the door,” said Holmes.

“Oh, indeed! You seem to have done the thing very completely. I must compliment you.”

“And I you,” Holmes answered. “Your red-headed idea was very new and effective.”

“You’ll see your pal again presently,” said Jones. “He’s quicker at climbing down holes than I am. Just hold out while I fix the derbies.”

“I beg that you will not touch me with your filthy hands,” remarked our prisoner as the handcuffs clattered upon his wrists. “You may not be aware that I have royal blood in my veins. Have the goodness, also, when you address me always to say ‘sir’ and ‘please.’”

“All right,” said Jones with a stare and a snigger. “Well, would you please, sir, march upstairs, where we can get a cab to carry your Highness to the police-station?”

“That is better,” said John Clay serenely. He made a sweeping bow to the three of us and walked quietly off in the custody of the detective.

“Really, Mr. Holmes,” said Mr. Merryweather as we followed them from the cellar, “I do not know how the bank can thank you or repay you. There is no doubt that you have detected and defeated in the most complete manner one of the most determined attempts at bank robbery that have ever come within my experience.”

blocks.text:
Portal's plot is revealed to the player via audio messages or "announcements" from GLaDOS and visual elements inside rooms found in later levels. According to The Final Hours of Portal 2, the year is established to be "somewhere in 2010"—twelve years after Aperture Science has been abandoned.

The game begins with Chell waking up from a stasis bed and hearing instructions and warnings from GLaDOS, an artificial intelligence, about upcoming tests. Chell enters into distinct chambers that introduce players to the game's mechanics, sequentially. GLaDOS's announcements serve as instructions to Chell and help the player progress through the game, but also develops the atmosphere and characterizes the AI as a person. Chell is promised cake as her reward if she completes all test chambers.

Chell proceeds through the empty Enrichment Center, with GLaDOS as her only interaction. As the player nears completion, GLaDOS's motives and behavior turn more sinister; although she is designed to appear encouraging, GLaDOS's actions and speech suggest insincerity and callous disregard for the safety and well-being of the test subjects. The test chambers become increasingly dangerous as Chell proceeds, tests including a live-fire course designed for military androids, as well as some chambers flooded with a hazardous liquid. In another chamber, GLaDOS notes the importance of the Weighted Companion Cube, a waist-high crate with a single large pink heart on each face, for helping Chell to complete the test.

blocks.text:
The Taxi deal with ABC included a television special/pilot for Kaufman. He proposed Andy's Funhouse, based on a routine that he had developed while in junior college. The special was taped in 1977 but did not air until August 1979. It featured most of Andy's famous gags, including Foreign Man/Latka and his Elvis Presley impersonation, as well as a host of unique segments (including a special appearance by children's television character Howdy Doody and the "Has-been Corner"). The program also included a segment with fake television screen static as part of the gag, although ABC executives feared that viewers would mistake the static for broadcast problems and would change the channel—which was the comic element that Kaufman wanted to present. Andy's Funhouse was written by Kaufman, Zmuda and Mel Sherer, with music by Kaufman.

In March 1980, Kaufman filmed a short segment for an ABC show called Buckshot. The segment was just over six minutes long and was called Uncle Andy's Funhouse. It featured Kaufman as the host of a children's show for adults, complete with a peanut gallery and Tony Clifton puppet.

teaching.en: Compare an apparent message with its function in the complete reported context. Ask what the communication invites someone to do, and test that reading against actions, qualifications and the audience’s possible interpretation. Keep the creator’s purpose, another person’s interpretation and an observed outcome separate. “Suggest” and “feared” do not confirm every motive or every audience response. Background: Portal is a fictional game; Chell is the test subject and GLaDOS the guiding AI. A chamber is a room, stasis is a resting state, and a live-fire course uses weapons. The other account describes television entertainment: static is screen noise, a gag is a joke, a pilot is a trial programme, and a peanut gallery is an on-stage audience. Programme titles identify productions; no song lyrics or game dialogue are required.

workedExample.en: Unscored invented example: “Will you chair the meeting?” asks Arun. Mei thinks she dislikes how the agenda was imposed, but says, “My calendar is rather full.” Arun offers a later date. Mei replies, “Thank you, but please ask someone else.” The first answer indirectly declines while withholding the agenda objection; Arun initially hears a scheduling problem. The final refusal rules out accepting a later slot. It does not prove that Mei’s calendar was empty.
workedExample.zh-Hans: 不计分虚构示例：Arun问：“Will you chair the meeting?” Mei心想自己不喜欢被强加的议程，却说：“My calendar is rather full.” Arun提议改期。Mei回答：“Thank you, but please ask someone else.” 第一次答复间接拒绝，同时没有说出议程方面的顾虑；Arun起初理解成时间问题。最后的拒绝排除了接受改期，但不能证明Mei的日程原本空闲。

questions.prompt: Which interpretation distinguishes the apparent message from its supported communicative purpose and the audience’s understanding?
options: The instructions and reward promise encourage Chell to keep participating, while the growing danger makes a purely caring interpretation unreliable. The account presents increasing signs of insincerity; it does not confirm delivery of the cake or explain the behaviour as an accidental malfunction.

The cake promise establishes that the reward has already been delivered. The dangerous chambers prove GLaDOS has stopped giving instructions, and every announcement is an openly stated request that Chell leave the centre immediately.

Because the announcements sound encouraging, GLaDOS is established as sincerely protecting every test subject. The hazards are reported as accidental malfunctions, so the source gives no reason to question the apparent benevolence.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation distinguishes the apparent message from its supported communicative purpose and the audience’s understanding?
options: The static is an accidental broadcast failure that Kaufman tried to repair. The executives confirm every viewer stayed on the channel, while the later children’s-show format proves that both programmes were designed solely to instruct children.

Kaufman’s comic purpose guarantees that every viewer recognized the fake static immediately. The executives’ fear is his own wish to remove the gag, and the later adult audience means that the children’s-show format was absent.

The static deliberately makes an apparent broadcast fault part of a joke. The executives’ fear describes a possible audience response, not proof viewers actually changed channels. The later children’s-show format is for adults, so familiar presentation does not by itself identify the intended communicative purpose or audience.

explanations.zh-Hans: 原文说静电画面是伪装且属于笑料，并非意外故障。担心观众换台不等于证实他们留下；后一个节目虽用儿童节目形式，却明确面向成人。
explanations.zh-Hant: 原文說靜電畫面是偽裝且屬於笑料，並非意外故障。擔心觀眾換台不等於證實他們留下；後一個節目雖用兒童節目形式，卻明確面向成人。
explanations.en: The source calls the static fake and part of a gag, not an accidental fault. A feared channel change is not a confirmed decision to stay; the later programme explicitly addresses adults, despite its children’s-show form.

explanations.zh-Hans: 创作者的用意不能保证观众如何理解。高管的顾虑与Kaufman想呈现的喜剧效果不同；成人受众也不意味着材料所述儿童节目形式不存在。
explanations.zh-Hant: 創作者的用意不能保證觀眾如何理解。高管的顧慮與Kaufman想呈現的喜劇效果不同；成人受眾也不意味著材料所述兒童節目形式不存在。
explanations.en: A creator’s purpose cannot guarantee the audience’s interpretation. The executives’ concern and Kaufman’s desired comic element are distinct; an adult audience does not remove the reported children’s-show format.
